title.zh: 卷一百〇九 列傳第三十九: 伶官 宦官
title.en: Volume 109 Biographies 39: Music and Imperial Officials
title.raw: 卷一百〇九 列傳第三十九: 伶官 宦官 Volume 109 Biographies 39: Music and Imperial Officials

sentences.zh: 伶官 ○羅衣輕

translations.literal: Music Officials ○ Luo Yiqing
translations.idiomatic: Music Officials ○ Luo Yiqing

sentences.zh: 伶，官之微者也。

translations.literal: Music performers are the most humble of officials.
translations.idiomatic: Court entertainers ranked among the lowest offices in the hierarchy.

sentences.zh: 《五代史》列鏡新磨於《傳》，是必有所取矣。

translations.literal: The History of the Five Dynasties lists Jing Xinmo in a biography—there must have been reason to include him.
translations.idiomatic: The History of the Five Dynasties devoted a full biography to the entertainer Jing Xinmo, which shows that such figures could merit historical notice.

sentences.zh: 遼之伶官當時固多，然能因詼諧示諫，以消未形之亂，惟羅衣輕耳。

translations.literal: Liao music officials were indeed numerous at the time, yet only Luo Yiqing could use jest and wit to offer remonstrance and dispel disorder before it took shape.
translations.idiomatic: The Liao court had many entertainers, but only Luo Yiqing turned humor into counsel and defused brewing crises before they broke out.

sentences.zh: 孔子曰：「君子不以人廢言。」

translations.literal: Confucius said: "The gentleman does not reject words because of the person who speaks them."
translations.idiomatic: Confucius said, "A gentleman does not dismiss a saying merely because of who said it."

sentences.zh: 是宜傳。

translations.literal: Therefore he deserves a biography.
translations.idiomatic: For that reason he deserves a place in the annals.

sentences.zh: 羅衣輕，不知其鄉里。

translations.literal: Luo Yiqing—his native place is unknown.
translations.idiomatic: Luo Yiqing's place of origin is not recorded.

sentences.zh: 滑稽通變，一時諧謔，多所規諷。

translations.literal: Witty and resourceful, for a time the foremost in jest and banter, he offered much indirect remonstrance.
translations.idiomatic: Quick-witted and adaptable, he was the leading comic at court and often couched admonition in playful speech.

sentences.zh: 興宗敗於李元昊也，單騎突出，幾不得脫。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xingzong was defeated by Li Yuanhao, he broke through alone on horseback and barely escaped.
translations.idiomatic: After Emperor Xingzong's defeat at the hands of Li Yuanhao of Western Xia, he fled the field alone and nearly failed to get away.

sentences.zh: 先是，元昊獲遼人，輒劓其鼻，有奔北者惟恐追及。

translations.literal: Earlier, whenever Yuanhao captured men of Liao, he would slice off their noses; those who fled north feared only that pursuers would catch them.
translations.idiomatic: Before this, Yuanhao had captured Liao soldiers and routinely mutilated their noses, so men fleeing homeward lived in terror of being overtaken.

sentences.zh: 故羅衣輕止之曰：「且觀鼻在否？」

translations.literal: Therefore Luo Yiqing stopped him and said: "First let us see whether your nose is still there."
translations.idiomatic: Luo Yiqing therefore halted him and quipped, "Let us first check whether your nose is still in place."

sentences.zh: 上怒，以毳索系帳後，將殺之。

translations.literal: The emperor was enraged, tied him with a fur rope behind the tent, and was about to execute him.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor flew into a rage, bound him with a fur cord behind the tent, and prepared to put him to death.

sentences.zh: 太子笑曰：「打諢底不是黃幡綽！」

translations.literal: The crown prince laughed and said: "The one doing the comic patter is no Huang Fanchuo!"
translations.idiomatic: The crown prince laughed and said, "The fellow cracking jokes is no Huang Fanchuo!"

sentences.zh: 羅衣輕應聲曰：「行兵底亦不是唐太宗！」

translations.literal: Luo Yiqing answered on the spot: "The one leading troops in the field is no Emperor Taizong of Tang either!"
translations.idiomatic: Luo Yiqing shot back at once, "And the one commanding the army is no Emperor Taizong of Tang either!"

sentences.zh: 上聞而釋之。

translations.literal: When the emperor heard this, he released him.
translations.idiomatic: Hearing this, the emperor set him free.

sentences.zh: 上嘗與太弟重元狎昵，宴酣，許以千秋萬歲後傳位。

translations.literal: The emperor had once been on intimate terms with his younger brother Chongyuan; when the feast grew merry, he promised to pass the throne to him after a thousand autumns and ten thousand years.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor had grown overly familiar with his younger brother Chongyuan; deep in wine at a banquet, he promised to abdicate in his favor in the distant future.

sentences.zh: 重元喜甚，驕縱不法。

translations.literal: Chongyuan was overjoyed and grew arrogant and lawless.
translations.idiomatic: Chongyuan was elated and became arrogant and unrestrained.

sentences.zh: 又因雙陸，賭以居民城邑。

translations.literal: They also wagered at backgammon, staking towns and their inhabitants.
translations.idiomatic: They also played backgammon, wagering whole towns and their populations.

sentences.zh: 帝屢不競，前後已償數城。

translations.literal: The emperor repeatedly lost and had already paid over several cities.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor lost again and again and had already forfeited several cities.

sentences.zh: 重元既恃梁孝王之寵，又多鄭叔段之過，朝臣無敢言者，道路以目。

translations.literal: Chongyuan both relied on favor like Prince Xiao of Liang and committed faults like Duke Zhuang's younger brother Shuduan; court officials dared not speak, and people on the road exchanged glances in fear.
translations.idiomatic: Chongyuan enjoyed favor comparable to Prince Xiao of Liang under Emperor Wen of Han and repeated the overreaching of Duke Zhuang's brother Shuduan; no minister dared remonstrate, and travelers only dared signal their alarm with their eyes.

sentences.zh: 一日復博，羅衣輕指其局曰：「雙陸休癡，和你都輸去也！」

translations.literal: One day they were gambling again; Luo Yiqing pointed at the board and said: "Stop being mad about backgammon—you will lose everything to him!"
translations.idiomatic: One day they were at the board again; Luo Yiqing pointed at the game and said, "Enough of this backgammon folly—you are going to lose everything to him!"

sentences.zh: 帝始悟，不復戲。

translations.literal: The emperor then understood and no longer played.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor finally took the point and gave up the game.

sentences.zh: 清寧間，以疾卒。

translations.literal: During the Qingning era he died of illness.
translations.idiomatic: He died of illness during the Qingning period.

sentences.zh: ◎宦官 ○王繼恩趙安仁

translations.literal: ◎ Eunuch Officials ○ Wang Jien and Zhao Anren
translations.idiomatic: ◎ Eunuch Officials ○ Wang Jien and Zhao Anren

sentences.zh: 《周禮》，寺人掌中門之禁。

translations.literal: In the Rites of Zhou, palace stewards guard the inner gates.
translations.idiomatic: The Rites of Zhou assign palace stewards to guard the inner gates.

sentences.zh: 至巷伯詩列於《雅》，勃貂功著於晉，雖忠於所事，而非其職矣。

translations.literal: By the time the Palace Steward ode was placed among the Greater Odes, and Bo Diao's achievements were celebrated in Jin, though loyal to those they served, this was no longer their proper office.
translations.idiomatic: Later the "Palace Steward" ode entered the Greater Odes, and Bo Diao won fame in Jin—loyal to their masters, perhaps, but already acting outside their proper charge.

sentences.zh: 漢、唐中世，竊權蠹政，有不忍言者，是皆寵遇之過。

translations.literal: In the middle periods of Han and Tang, they usurped power and ruined government—there are things one cannot bear to recount—all excesses of favor.
translations.idiomatic: In the middle Han and Tang periods eunuchs seized power and poisoned government, producing scandals too grim to relate in full—all the result of excessive favor.

sentences.zh: 遼宦者二人，其賢不肖皆可為後世鑒，故傳焉。

translations.literal: Two Liao eunuchs—the worthy and the unworthy alike may serve as mirrors for later ages; therefore they are given biographies.
translations.idiomatic: Liao produced two eunuchs whose conduct, good and bad, can instruct posterity; that is why they are recorded here.

sentences.zh: 王繼恩，棣州人。

translations.literal: Wang Jien was a native of Dizhou.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Jien came from Dizhou.

sentences.zh: 睿智皇后南征，繼恩被俘。

translations.literal: When Empress Ruizhi campaigned south, Jien was captured.
translations.idiomatic: When Empress Ruizhi marched south, Jien was taken prisoner.

sentences.zh: 初，皇后以公私所獲十歲已下兒容貌可觀者近百人，載赴涼陘，並使閹為豎，繼恩在焉。

translations.literal: At first the empress took nearly a hundred children under ten years of age, of pleasing appearance, gained through public and private means, conveyed them to Liangjin, and had them all castrated to serve as attendants; Jien was among them.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier the empress had gathered nearly a hundred children under ten, handsome boys taken in raids and by other means, sent them to Liangjin, and had them all castrated as palace attendants; Jien was one of them.

sentences.zh: 聰慧，通書及遼語。

translations.literal: Intelligent and clever, he mastered books and the Khitan language.
translations.idiomatic: Clever and quick to learn, he mastered written Chinese and the Khitan language.

sentences.zh: 擢內謁者、內侍左廂押班。

translations.literal: He was promoted to Inner Attendant and chief of the left wing of the Inner Service.
translations.idiomatic: He rose to Inner Attendant and chief steward of the left wing of the inner palace.

sentences.zh: 聖宗親政，累遷尚衣庫使、左承宣、監門衛大將軍、靈州觀察使、內庫都提點。

translations.literal: When Emperor Shengzong took personal rule, he was repeatedly promoted—to Director of the Imperial Wardrobe, Left Commissioner of Announcement, Grand General of the Gate Guards, Military Commissioner of Lingzhou, and Chief Intendant of the Inner Treasury.
translations.idiomatic: After Emperor Shengzong assumed personal rule, Jien was promoted in succession to Director of the Imperial Wardrobe, Left Commissioner of Announcement, Grand General of the Gate Guards, Military Commissioner of Lingzhou, and Chief Intendant of the Inner Treasury.

sentences.zh: 繼恩好清談，不喜權利，每得賜賚，市書至萬卷，載以自隨，誦讀不倦。

translations.literal: Jien loved pure conversation and disliked power and profit; whenever he received gifts, he would buy books by the ten thousand scrolls, carry them with him, and read without tiring.
translations.idiomatic: Jien loved scholarly talk and cared nothing for power or gain; whenever he received rewards he bought books by the thousands, carried them wherever he went, and read without cease.

sentences.zh: 每宋使來聘，繼恩多充宣賜使。

translations.literal: Whenever Song envoys came on embassy, Jien often served as commissioner of gifts and grants.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever Song envoys arrived on diplomatic missions, Jien was often appointed to distribute imperial gifts.

sentences.zh: 後不知所終。

translations.literal: Later his end is unknown.
translations.idiomatic: What became of him afterward is not recorded.

sentences.zh: 趙安仁，字小喜，深州樂壽人，自幼被俘。

translations.literal: Zhao Anren, style name Xiaoxi, a native of Leshou in Shenzhou, was captured while still a child.
translations.idiomatic: Zhao Anren, whose style was Xiaoxi, came from Leshou in Shenzhou and had been taken captive as a boy.

sentences.zh: 統和中，為黃門令、秦晉國王府祗候。

translations.literal: During the Tonghe era he served as Yellow Gate Commandant and attendant at the mansion of the Prince of Qin and Jin.
translations.idiomatic: During the Tonghe reign he served as Yellow Gate Commandant and attendant at the mansion of the Prince of Qin and Jin.

sentences.zh: 王薨，授內侍省押班、禦院通進。

translations.literal: When the prince died, he was appointed chief of the Inner Attendant Service and Imperial Park courier.
translations.idiomatic: After the prince's death he was appointed chief steward of the Inner Attendant Service and courier of the Imperial Park.

sentences.zh: 開泰八年，與李勝哥謀奔南土，為遊兵所擒。

translations.literal: In the eighth year of Kaitai, he plotted with Li Shengge to flee to the southern lands and was seized by roving troops.
translations.idiomatic: In the eighth year of Kaitai he plotted with Li Shengge to escape south and was caught by patrol troops.

sentences.zh: 初，仁德皇后與欽哀有隙，欽哀密令安仁伺皇后動靜，無不知者。

translations.literal: Earlier, Empress Rende and Qintian were at odds; Qintian secretly ordered Anren to watch the empress's movements—nothing escaped his knowledge.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier Empress Rende and Empress Dowager Qintian were estranged; Qintian secretly set Anren to spy on the empress's every move, and nothing escaped him.

sentences.zh: 仁德皇后威權既重，安仁懼禍，復謀亡歸。

translations.literal: Once Empress Rende's authority had grown heavy, Anren feared disaster and again plotted to flee home.
translations.idiomatic: When Empress Rende's power grew formidable, Anren feared for his life and again plotted to escape south.

sentences.zh: 仁德欲誅之，欽哀以言營救。

translations.literal: Rende wished to execute him; Qintian pleaded on his behalf.
translations.idiomatic: Rende sought to have him executed, but Qintian interceded for him.

sentences.zh: 聖宗曰：「小喜言父母兄弟俱在南朝，每一念，神魂隕越。

translations.literal: Emperor Shengzong said: "Xiaoxi says that his parents and brothers are all in the Southern Court; at every thought his spirit and soul are overwhelmed.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Shengzong said, "Xiaoxi reports that his parents and brothers all remain in the Song realm; the mere thought of them overwhelms his spirit.

sentences.zh: 今為思親，冒死而亡，亦孝子用心，實可憐憫。」

translations.literal: Now, longing for kin, he risked death to flee—this too is a filial son's heart and truly deserves pity."
translations.idiomatic: Now, moved by love for his family, he risked death to flee. That is the heart of a filial son and truly calls for compassion."

sentences.zh: 赦之。

translations.literal: He was pardoned.
translations.idiomatic: He was pardoned.

sentences.zh: 重熙初，欽哀攝政，欲廢帝，立少子重元。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Chongxi, Qintian acted as regent, wished to depose the emperor, and install her younger son Chongyuan.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Chongxi era Empress Dowager Qintian served as regent, sought to depose the emperor, and planned to enthrone her younger son Chongyuan.

sentences.zh: 帝與安仁謀，遷太后慶州守陵，授安仁左承宣、監門衛大將軍，充契丹漢人渤海內侍都知，兼都提點。

translations.literal: The emperor plotted with Anren, moved the empress dowager to Qingzhou to guard the tombs, and appointed Anren Left Commissioner of Announcement, Grand General of the Gate Guards, and superintendent of Khitan, Han, and Bohai inner attendants, also chief intendant.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor conspired with Anren, sent the empress dowager to Qingzhou to tend the imperial tombs, and appointed Anren Left Commissioner of Announcement and Grand General of the Gate Guards, making him superintendent of Khitan, Han, and Bohai inner attendants and chief intendant as well.

sentences.zh: 會上思太后，親馭奉迎，太后責曰：」汝負萬死，我嘗營救。

translations.literal: When the emperor came to miss the empress dowager and personally drove out to welcome her back, the empress dowager rebuked him: "You deserve ten thousand deaths; I once pleaded for your life."
translations.idiomatic: When the emperor missed his mother and went in person to escort her back, the empress dowager reproached him: "You deserved death a thousand times over, yet I once saved your life."

sentences.zh: 不望汝報，何為離間我母子耶！」

translations.literal: I did not expect repayment from you—why have you driven a wedge between mother and son!"
translations.idiomatic: I asked for no reward—why have you driven us mother and son apart!"

sentences.zh: 安仁無答。

translations.literal: Anren had no reply.
translations.idiomatic: Anren had nothing to say.

sentences.zh: 後不知所終。

translations.literal: Later his end is unknown.
translations.idiomatic: What became of him afterward is not recorded.

sentences.zh: 論曰：名器所以礪天下，非賢而有功則不可授，況宦者乎！

translations.literal: Commentary says: Titles and regalia are what hone the realm; if one is not worthy and has no merit, they must not be granted—how much more so for eunuchs!
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Honorary titles and insignia exist to sharpen the realm's virtue; they must not be granted without merit and worthiness—and least of all to eunuchs.

sentences.zh: 繼恩為內謁者，安仁為黃門令，似矣，何至溺於私愛，而授以觀察使、大將軍耶？

translations.literal: Jien as Inner Attendant and Anren as Yellow Gate Commandant would seem fitting enough—how could favoritism go so far as to grant them military commissioner and grand general?
translations.idiomatic: Jien as Inner Attendant and Anren as Yellow Gate Commandant would have been fitting enough—how could private affection run so deep that they were made military commissioners and grand generals?

sentences.zh: 《易》曰：「負且乘，致寇至。」

translations.literal: The Book of Changes says: "He bears a burden yet rides in a carriage—robbers will come."
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Changes says, "He carries a burden yet rides in a carriage—bandits will come upon him."

sentences.zh: 此安仁所以不克有終，繼恩幸而免歟？

translations.literal: This is why Anren could not see his course through to the end, while Jien was fortunate to escape—is it not?
translations.idiomatic: Is this not why Anren failed to end well, while Jien was fortunate enough to escape a similar fate?
